angle: 25 money lessons rich parents teach their kids, from 3 angles: numbers, psychology, playbook
title: 25 Money Lessons Rich Parents Teach Their Kids

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. Most of us learned about money the hard way. A first credit card, a first car loan, a first month where the paycheck ran out before the bills did. Nobody sat us down and explained how any of it worked. But in many wealthy families, kids learn these lessons at the kitchen table, years before they ever earn a paycheck. Today, twenty five money lessons rich parents teach their kids. And here's the good news. You can teach them to your kids, and you can learn them yourself, at any age.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's why this matters so much. Researchers at the University of Cambridge, in a study for the UK's Money Advice Service, found that many core money habits are already forming by around age seven.

card.label: age when money habits start forming
card.sub: University of Cambridge, for the Money Advice Service (2013)

scenes.short_hook: Most kids never learn this at school. Rich kids learn it at home.

scenes.text: Think about that. By the time a child is in second grade, they're already picking up attitudes about saving, spending and waiting for things they want. Most of those attitudes come from watching their parents. Not from lectures. From what happens in the grocery store, at the car dealership and around the dinner table. That's why the money lessons in a family get passed down, generation after generation, whether anyone intends to teach them or not.
scenes.query: Child with piggy bank at home
scenes.caption: HABITS START EARLY

scenes.text: We'll look at these twenty five lessons from three angles. First, the numbers. The basic math of money that many wealthy families teach early, like compound interest and opportunity cost. Second, the psychology. The attitudes about waiting, comparing and enough that shape a lifetime of decisions. And third, the playbook. The practical tools, from first investment accounts to credit scores, that give kids a head start. Whether you're a parent, a grandparent, or someone who wishes they'd learned this at twelve, there's something here for you.
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: Let's start with the numbers. Lesson one is the foundation of everything else.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Our sources. The research on when money habits form comes from the University of Cambridge's study for the Money Advice Service. Data on how families talk about money comes from T. Rowe Price's Parents, Kids and Money Survey. Research on giving money to adult children comes from Thomas Stanley's work in The Millionaire Next Door. Account rules come from the IRS. Growth examples use a stated seven percent average yearly return, an illustration, not a promise. This is education, not financial advice.
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Nine lessons about how money actually works, taught in ways a kid can understand.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Lesson number one. Money comes from creating value for other people.
scenes.caption: LESSON 1

scenes.text: Many wealthy parents make sure their kids understand where money comes from. It doesn't come from the ATM or from a card. It comes from someone doing something valuable for someone else. That might be a job, a business, or an investment in a business. Kids who understand this early tend to see money as something they can create, not just something they receive.
scenes.caption: MONEY IS EARNED

scenes.text: Some families pay for extra chores beyond the basics, like washing the car or helping with yard work. Others encourage teenagers to get part time jobs, even when the family doesn't need the money. The point isn't the amount. It's the connection between effort, value and reward. A teenager who earns their first hundred dollars often treats it very differently from a hundred dollars that was simply handed over.
scenes.caption: EFFORT, VALUE, REWARD

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Pick one extra job around the house that a child can do for pay. Talk about why it's worth money. Someone would otherwise have to do it, or pay someone else to. If you're an adult learning this lesson yourself, ask the same question about your job. What value do I create, and how could I create more?
scenes.caption: ONE PAID JOB THIS WEEK

scenes.text: Lesson number two. Save first, then spend what's left.
scenes.caption: LESSON 2

scenes.text: A classic teaching tool is three jars, labeled save, spend and give. Every time a child gets money, whether it's an allowance, a gift or pay for a chore, it's split between the jars before anything is spent. It's simple, visual and surprisingly powerful, because it builds the habit of paying yourself first before a child ever sees a paycheck.
scenes.caption: SAVE, SPEND, GIVE

scenes.text: Adults who pay themselves first, by automatically moving money to savings on payday, tend to save far more than those who save whatever is left at the end of the month. The three jars are the childhood version of exactly that system. Kids who grow up with it often find automatic saving completely natural as adults.
scenes.caption: PAY YOURSELF FIRST

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Set up three jars or three envelopes. Decide on a split together, for example fifty percent spend, forty percent save, ten percent give. Let the child choose what to do with the spend jar, even if they make choices you wouldn't. For yourself, set up one automatic transfer to savings the day after payday.
scenes.caption: SET UP THE JARS

scenes.text: Lesson number three. Money can grow on its own, if you give it time.
scenes.caption: LESSON 3

scenes.text: Compound interest is when your money earns returns, and then those returns earn returns too. Over time, the growth snowballs. Many wealthy parents explain it early, because time is the most powerful ingredient, and kids have more time than anyone. A dollar invested at fifteen has fifty years to grow before a typical retirement age.
scenes.caption: MONEY THAT GROWS

scenes.text: Some parents make it concrete with a family bank. They offer a generous interest rate on money the child leaves with them, maybe paid monthly. Watching a balance grow without doing anything is a magical moment for a kid. It turns an abstract idea into something they can see. Others show a simple chart of what a small monthly investment becomes over decades.
scenes.query: Parent and child with tablet chart
scenes.caption: THE FAMILY BANK

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Use a free online compound interest calculator with your child. Try one hundred dollars a month at a seven percent average yearly return, for ten, twenty and fifty years. Let them see how the line curves upward. For yourself, run the same numbers on your own savings.
scenes.caption: RUN THE NUMBERS

scenes.text: Here's what that looks like. One hundred dollars a month, starting at age fifteen and invested until sixty five, at a seven percent average yearly return, could grow to over five hundred thousand dollars. Total put in, sixty thousand.
Lesson number four. Interest works against you when you borrow.
scenes.caption: LESSON 4

scenes.text: The same math that grows savings can grow debt. Wealthy parents often make sure their kids understand this before they get their first credit card. A card balance at over twenty percent interest, which has been typical in recent years according to the Federal Reserve, can grow quickly if you only make minimum payments.
scenes.caption: DEBT COMPOUNDS TOO
scenes.short_hook: Interest can make you rich. It can also make you broke.

scenes.text: A powerful way to teach this is to let a child borrow a small amount from you, for something they want now, and charge them interest. When they have to pay back twelve dollars for a ten dollar loan, the lesson sticks far better than any lecture. Some families do the reverse too, and show how long it takes to pay off a balance with minimum payments.
scenes.caption: CHARGE A LITTLE INTEREST

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Look at a real credit card statement together and find the box that shows how long it would take to pay off the balance with minimum payments. For yourself, list every debt you have with its interest rate, and target the highest rate first.
scenes.query: Credit card statement minimum payment box
scenes.caption: READ THE WARNING BOX

scenes.text: Lesson number five. The price isn't the same as the value.
scenes.caption: LESSON 5

scenes.text: Rich parents often teach kids to think about cost per use. A sixty dollar pair of shoes worn three hundred times costs twenty cents a wear. A thirty dollar pair worn five times costs six dollars a wear. The cheaper item was actually more expensive. This simple idea helps kids judge purchases by how much they'll really use them.
scenes.caption: COST PER USE

scenes.text: It also works the other way. Some things are expensive and still not worth it, because they won't be used. The trendy gadget that sits in a drawer after a week. The toy that's forgotten by the next birthday. Asking how often will I use this before buying is one of the most useful money habits a person can have.
scenes.caption: PRICE ISN'T VALUE

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Before your child's next purchase, ask them to guess how many times they'll use it, then divide the price by that number. For yourself, try it on the five most expensive things in your closet or garage.
scenes.caption: DIVIDE BY USES

scenes.text: Lesson number six. Every time you spend, you're giving something else up.
scenes.caption: LESSON 6

scenes.text: Economists call it opportunity cost. If you spend twenty dollars on candy, you can't spend that twenty dollars on a game you've been saving for. Wealthy parents often teach this by making kids choose, rather than buying both. The question becomes not can I afford this, but what am I giving up to get it?
scenes.caption: WHAT ARE YOU GIVING UP?

scenes.text: For adults, the biggest opportunity cost is often future growth. A thousand dollars spent today is not just a thousand dollars. At a seven percent average yearly return, it could have roughly doubled about every ten years. That's why wealthy people often think twice before big purchases.
scenes.caption: OPPORTUNITY COST

scenes.text: Teach it this week. At the store, give your child a fixed amount and let them choose between two things they want. Talk about what they gave up. For yourself, before any purchase over a hundred dollars, say out loud what else that money could do.
scenes.caption: CHOOSE ONE

scenes.text: Lesson number seven. A budget is just a plan for your money.
scenes.caption: LESSON 7

scenes.text: Many financially savvy parents use an allowance as a teaching tool, not just pocket money. As kids get older, the allowance grows, and so do their responsibilities. A teenager might get a monthly amount that covers their clothes, entertainment and phone, and has to plan how to make it last.
scenes.caption: A PLAN FOR YOUR MONEY

scenes.text: This lets kids practice budgeting with small amounts, when mistakes are cheap. Running out of money in the middle of the month at fifteen is a valuable lesson. Running out at thirty five, with rent and kids, is much more painful.
scenes.caption: PRACTICE WITH SMALL MONEY

scenes.text: Teach it this week. If your child is old enough, give them responsibility for one category, like clothes or entertainment, with a fixed monthly amount. Let them plan and make mistakes. For yourself, write a one page plan for next month's money.
scenes.caption: ONE CATEGORY

scenes.text: Lesson number eight. What you earn isn't what you take home.
scenes.caption: LESSON 8

scenes.text: Many young adults are shocked by their first paycheck. The salary was one number, but the deposit was much smaller. Federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare, maybe state tax, health insurance and retirement contributions all come out first. Wealthy parents often walk their kids through a real pay stub before that first job.
scenes.caption: GROSS VS NET

scenes.text: Understanding gross versus net pay changes how young people budget, and how they think about job offers. It also introduces taxes, which play a huge role in wealth building. Kids who learn early that tax advantaged accounts exist often start using them much sooner.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST PAYCHECK SURPRISE

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Show your teenager one of your pay stubs, or a sample one online, and go line by line. What is each deduction? Where does it go? For yourself, check whether you're getting the full employer match on your retirement plan.
scenes.caption: GO LINE BY LINE

scenes.text: Lesson number nine. Owners build wealth. Customers pay for it.
scenes.caption: LESSON 9

scenes.text: When a kid buys a video game, they're a customer of that company. When they own shares of that company, they share in its profits. Wealthy families often teach this distinction early. They point out that broad index funds let ordinary people own small pieces of hundreds of companies.
scenes.caption: CUSTOMER OR OWNER?

scenes.text: Some parents buy a single share of a company their child loves, so the child can follow it and feel what it's like to be an owner. The goal isn't stock picking. It's understanding that you can be on the earning side of the economy, not just the spending side.
scenes.caption: OWN A PIECE

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Pick a few companies whose products your family uses every day. Look up their stock prices together and talk about what it means to own a piece of them. For yourself, ask what you own that generates income or growth.
scenes.caption: COMPANIES YOU USE

scenes.text: Before we move on, let's talk about why these number lessons so often get skipped. In surveys by T. Rowe Price, many parents have said they feel uncomfortable talking about money with their kids. Some feel they don't know enough. Others were raised to think money talk is impolite. Some don't want to worry their children.
scenes.caption: THE SKIPPED TALK
scenes.chapter: The money talk most families skip

scenes.text: But silence teaches too. When parents never talk about money, kids still learn from what they see. They see the new car, the shopping bags, the stress when a bill arrives. Without explanations, they fill in the blanks themselves, and often draw the wrong conclusions.
scenes.caption: SILENCE TEACHES TOO

scenes.text: You don't need to be an expert to have these conversations. You just need to be honest. Saying I made a mistake with credit cards when I was young, and here's what I learned, can be one of the most valuable lessons a child ever hears. Your mistakes are free tuition for your kids.
scenes.caption: YOUR MISTAKES ARE THEIR TUITION

scenes.text: That's angle one. Money is earned, save first, compound interest, interest on debt, price versus value, opportunity cost, budgeting, paychecks and ownership. Now angle two. The psychology. Because knowing the math isn't enough. The attitudes are what really get passed down.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The most important money lessons often aren't about numbers at all. They're about patience, comparison, security and what it means to have enough. Rich parents who raise financially healthy kids tend to focus as much on these attitudes as on the math.
scenes.caption: ATTITUDES MATTER MORE

scenes.text: Lesson number ten. Learning to wait.
scenes.caption: LESSON 10

scenes.text: When kids want something, wealthy parents often don't just buy it. They help the child save for it. Waiting weeks or months for a toy teaches patience, planning and the satisfaction of earning something. It's the childhood version of saving for a house or retirement.
scenes.query: Child looking at toy in store window
scenes.caption: LEARNING TO WAIT

scenes.text: The famous marshmallow studies suggested that children who could wait for a bigger reward did better later in life. Newer research has added nuance, showing family circumstances matter a lot. But the skill of waiting is still something families can practice together.
scenes.caption: THE MARSHMALLOW TEST

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Next time your child asks for something, make a savings chart and help them track their progress toward it. For yourself, try a thirty day wait before any non essential purchase over a hundred dollars.
scenes.caption: TRACK THE PROGRESS

scenes.text: Lesson number eleven. Someone will always have more.
scenes.caption: LESSON 11

scenes.text: Kids notice what their friends have. The newer phone, the bigger house, the cooler shoes. Wealthy parents often teach that comparison is a trap, because there's always someone with more. They focus their kids on their own goals instead.
scenes.caption: SOMEONE ALWAYS HAS MORE

scenes.text: Many quiet millionaires model this themselves. They live in modest homes and drive ordinary cars, even when they could afford more. Their kids learn that you don't need to show your wealth to have it.
scenes.caption: NO NEED TO SHOW IT

scenes.text: Teach it this week. When your child compares themselves with a friend, ask, what do you actually want, and why? For yourself, unfollow a few accounts that make you feel like you need more.
scenes.caption: FOCUS ON YOUR GOALS

scenes.text: Lesson number twelve. Money is something families talk about.
scenes.caption: LESSON 12

scenes.text: In many wealthy families, money is a normal topic. Kids hear their parents discuss investments, budgets and decisions. They learn the vocabulary early. Words like interest, dividend, net worth and budget feel familiar, not intimidating.
scenes.caption: A NORMAL TOPIC

scenes.text: Talking about money doesn't mean sharing every detail or burdening kids with adult worries. It means explaining decisions in age appropriate ways. We're not buying a new car because we'd rather save for your college. That one sentence teaches more than a semester of lectures.
scenes.caption: AGE APPROPRIATE

scenes.text: Teach it this week. At dinner, explain one money decision your family made recently, and why. For yourself, have one honest money conversation with a partner or friend.
scenes.caption: ONE HONEST CONVERSATION

scenes.text: Lesson number thirteen. Let them make small mistakes now.
scenes.caption: LESSON 13

scenes.text: Some of the best money lessons come from mistakes. Spending a whole allowance on the first day and having nothing left for the weekend. Buying a toy that breaks in a week. Wealthy parents often resist the urge to rescue kids from these small mistakes.
scenes.caption: A CHEAP LESSON

scenes.text: A twenty dollar mistake at ten is far cheaper than a twenty thousand dollar mistake at thirty. When kids experience the consequences of money choices while the stakes are small, they build judgment that protects them later.
scenes.caption: LET THEM FAIL SMALL

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Next time your child makes a money mistake, don't fix it. Ask what they learned and what they'd do differently. For yourself, write down your biggest money mistake and the lesson it taught you.
scenes.caption: WHAT DID YOU LEARN?

scenes.text: Lesson number fourteen. Knowing what's enough.
scenes.caption: LESSON 14

scenes.text: Some wealthy families talk openly about the idea of enough. Without a sense of enough, no amount of money ever feels like it's sufficient. There's always a bigger house, a nicer car, a better vacation. With it, people can enjoy what they have and make clearer choices.
scenes.caption: ENOUGH

scenes.text: Teaching kids about enough helps them resist endless consumption, and protects them from feeling poor no matter how much they earn. It's one of the most valuable gifts a parent can give.
scenes.caption: THERE'S ALWAYS MORE

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Ask your child, what would be enough for you? A toy, a phone, a room? Talk about how it feels to have enough. For yourself, write down what enough looks like for your family.
scenes.caption: WHAT IS ENOUGH?

scenes.text: Lesson number fifteen. Money is a tool, not a measure of a person.
scenes.caption: LESSON 15

scenes.text: Rich parents who raise grounded kids often teach that money doesn't make someone better or worse. It's a tool for security, freedom and helping others. Kids who see money as a scoreboard can grow up anxious or arrogant. Kids who see it as a tool tend to use it more wisely.
scenes.caption: A TOOL
scenes.short_hook: Your kids are watching how you treat money. Here's the lesson.

scenes.text: This lesson shows up in how parents talk about others. Do they admire people for their cars, or for their character? Kids notice. And they absorb those values far more from watching than from listening.
scenes.caption: CHARACTER OVER CARS

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Point out someone you admire for their kindness, work ethic or generosity, not their wealth. For yourself, notice when you judge people by what they own.
scenes.caption: WHO DO YOU ADMIRE?

scenes.text: Let me pause for a second. If you're finding this useful, whether you're a parent or just learning these lessons for yourself, please subscribe to Ryan Rover Money. It's free and it helps the channel reach more families. Now, lesson sixteen.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Lesson number sixteen. Give some of it away.
scenes.caption: LESSON 16

scenes.text: Many wealthy families make giving part of their money system from the very beginning. Remember the three jars. Save, spend and give. Kids learn that money can help others, and that generosity is part of a good life. Stanley found that many millionaires gave regularly to causes they cared about.
scenes.caption: GIVE SOME AWAY

scenes.text: Giving also changes how kids see their own money. It builds gratitude and perspective. And research on happiness has found that spending money on others can make people happier than spending it on themselves.
scenes.caption: GRATITUDE AND PERSPECTIVE

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Let your child choose a cause for their give jar. A local animal shelter, a food bank, a friend in need. For yourself, set a small regular giving amount, even five dollars a month.
scenes.caption: CHOOSE A CAUSE

scenes.text: Lesson number seventeen. Real wealth is usually quiet.
scenes.caption: LESSON 17

scenes.text: Many wealthy parents teach their kids not to talk about money outside the family, and not to show it off. It's partly about safety, and partly about values. They don't want their kids to feel superior, or to be targets for people who want something from them.
scenes.caption: WEALTH IS QUIET

scenes.text: This lesson also helps kids understand that the flashy people they see online aren't necessarily rich. As Morgan Housel wrote in The Psychology of Money, wealth is what you don't see. It's the money not spent.
scenes.caption: WHAT YOU DON'T SEE

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Talk with your kids about why it's wise to keep family finances private. For yourself, notice the difference between people who look rich and people who are financially secure.
scenes.caption: KEEP IT PRIVATE

scenes.text: Here's the hardest truth for parents. Kids learn far more from what you do than from what you say. You can explain compound interest perfectly, but if you buy everything on impulse, that's the lesson they'll keep. The Cambridge research found that kids pick up money habits largely by watching the adults around them.
scenes.caption: WATCHING, NOT LISTENING
scenes.chapter: How kids really learn: watching, not listening

scenes.text: That's actually good news. It means you don't need perfect lessons. You need to model the behavior. Let them see you compare prices, say no to an impulse buy, put money into savings, and give to others. Narrate your decisions out loud sometimes. I'd like that, but I'm going to wait and think about it.
scenes.caption: MODEL THE BEHAVIOR

scenes.text: And if your own money habits aren't where you want them, the best lesson might be letting kids watch you improve. Seeing a parent pay off debt, build savings and stick to a plan teaches resilience, and that it's never too late to change.
scenes.caption: LET THEM WATCH YOU IMPROVE

scenes.text: That's angle two. Waiting, not comparing, open money talk, small mistakes, enough, money as a tool, generosity and quiet wealth. Now angle three. The playbook. Eight practical tools wealthy parents use to give their kids a real financial head start.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The playbook lessons are where wealthy families often pull ahead. Not because they have secret tools, but because they know these tools exist and use them early. Most of them are available to any family.
scenes.caption: THE TOOLS

scenes.text: Lesson number eighteen. Open accounts early.
scenes.caption: LESSON 18

scenes.text: Many wealthy parents open savings and investment accounts for their kids. Custodial accounts let parents invest on a child's behalf. And if a child has earned income, from a job or babysitting, for example, they may be able to contribute to a custodial Roth IRA, up to the amount they earned or the annual limit, whichever is lower. Check the current IRS rules.
scenes.query: Teen opening bank account with parent
scenes.caption: START EARLY
scenes.short_hook: A teenager with a summer job can open this account.

scenes.text: A Roth IRA started in the teenage years has decades of potential tax free growth ahead of it. Even a few thousand dollars invested at fifteen can grow significantly by retirement. Some parents even match their kids' contributions, like an employer match.
scenes.caption: DECADES OF GROWTH

scenes.text: Teach it this week. If your teenager has a job, research custodial Roth IRA options with a brokerage. Consider matching part of what they contribute. For yourself, make sure you're using your own tax advantaged accounts.
scenes.caption: MATCH THEIR SAVINGS

scenes.text: Lesson number nineteen. Understand credit before you need it.

card.title: Credit basics
card.sub: build it before you need it

scenes.caption: LESSON 19

scenes.text: A credit score affects the interest rate on car loans and mortgages, and sometimes rental applications and insurance prices. Wealthy parents often explain how credit scores work before their kids leave home. Pay on time, keep balances low, and don't open too many accounts at once.
scenes.caption: BUILD IT EARLY

scenes.text: Some parents add their teenager as an authorized user on a card they manage responsibly. Depending on the card issuer, this can help the child start a credit history. Others help their young adult open a secured card and use it for one small bill paid in full every month.
scenes.query: Parent and teen with credit card
scenes.caption: AUTHORIZED USER

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Show your teen what a credit score is and pull your own free credit report together at annualcreditreport.com. For yourself, set every card to autopay at least the minimum, so you're never late.
scenes.caption: CHECK YOUR REPORT

scenes.text: Lesson number twenty. You can ask for a better deal.
scenes.caption: LESSON 20

scenes.text: Wealthy parents often let their kids watch them negotiate, whether it's a car price, a phone bill, or a contract. Kids learn that the first number isn't always final, and that a polite question can save real money.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST NUMBER ISN'T FINAL

scenes.text: Negotiation is also a career skill. Research has shown that starting salaries affect a lifetime of earnings, because raises are often based on what you already make. Young people who negotiate their first salary can benefit for years.
scenes.query: Parent on phone with child listening
scenes.caption: LET THEM WATCH

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Let your kids listen while you call to ask for a lower rate on a bill. Talk afterward about what worked. For yourself, research the salary range for your role before your next review.
scenes.caption: KNOW YOUR WORTH

scenes.text: Lesson number twenty one. Protect what you build.
scenes.caption: LESSON 21

scenes.text: Rich families tend to understand insurance. Not insuring everything, but protecting against disasters that would be financially devastating. Health insurance, car insurance, renters or homeowners insurance, and life insurance when others depend on you.
scenes.caption: PROTECT WHAT YOU BUILD

scenes.text: Young adults often skip renters insurance or choose the bare minimum car coverage to save money. Then one accident or theft sets them back years. Teaching kids how insurance works before they leave home can prevent that.
scenes.caption: ONE ACCIDENT

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Walk your teen through your car or home insurance policy. What does it cover? What's a deductible? For yourself, check that your coverage still fits your life.
scenes.caption: WHAT'S A DEDUCTIBLE?

scenes.text: Lesson number twenty two. Try starting something of your own.
scenes.caption: LESSON 22

scenes.text: Many self made millionaires started small businesses as kids. Lemonade stands, lawn mowing, selling crafts, reselling items online. Stanley found that many millionaires were business owners. Early entrepreneurship teaches pricing, customer service, costs and profit.
scenes.caption: THE LEMONADE STAND

scenes.text: Even a tiny business teaches lessons a classroom can't. What happens when you price too high? Too low? What are your costs? What did you actually make after expenses? Those questions build business thinking that lasts a lifetime.
scenes.caption: COSTS AND PROFIT

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Help your child start a tiny business, even for one weekend. Track costs, sales and profit together. For yourself, consider one skill you could turn into a small side income.
scenes.caption: TRACK THE PROFIT

scenes.text: Lesson number twenty three. If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.
scenes.caption: LESSON 23

scenes.text: Scams target every age, including teenagers and young adults, often through social media, gaming platforms and texts. The Federal Trade Commission has reported that younger adults report losing money to fraud more often than older adults in some categories, even if older adults tend to lose larger amounts.
scenes.caption: TOO GOOD TO BE TRUE
scenes.short_hook: Teach your kids these three questions before they get scammed.

scenes.text: Wealthy parents teach kids to be skeptical of guaranteed returns, urgent deadlines, requests for gift cards, and anyone asking for passwords or codes. These red flags apply to almost every scam.
scenes.caption: RED FLAGS

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Share three questions with your kids. Is someone rushing me? Are they asking for gift cards, crypto or codes? Does it promise easy money? If yes to any, stop and ask a parent. For yourself, use the same questions.
scenes.caption: THREE QUESTIONS

scenes.text: Lesson number twenty four. Have a plan for the family.
scenes.caption: LESSON 24

scenes.text: Wealthy families usually have wills, named beneficiaries on accounts, and sometimes trusts. Many explain the basics to their kids as they grow up, so the next generation understands how wealth is protected and passed on.
scenes.caption: THE FAMILY PLAN

scenes.text: Every family can do the basics. A will, beneficiaries on retirement accounts and life insurance, and a plan for who would care for young children. These aren't just for the rich. They protect any family from confusion and conflict.
scenes.caption: NOT JUST FOR THE RICH

scenes.text: Teach it this week. If your kids are older, explain in simple terms what a will is and why it matters. For yourself, check the beneficiaries on every account you have.
scenes.caption: CHECK YOUR BENEFICIARIES

scenes.text: And lesson number twenty five. Rich parents don't give their kids everything.
scenes.caption: LESSON 25

scenes.text: This one surprises people. In The Millionaire Next Door, Stanley described what he called economic outpatient care, the substantial financial gifts some parents give to their adult children. His research suggested that adult children who received large ongoing gifts often accumulated less wealth than similar people who didn't.
scenes.caption: INDEPENDENCE IS THE GIFT

scenes.text: The lesson many wealthy parents take from this is that independence is the real gift. They help with education or a first home, perhaps, but they don't fund an entire lifestyle. They want their kids to know how to earn, save and build on their own.
scenes.caption: ECONOMIC OUTPATIENT CARE

scenes.text: Teach it this week. Think about one thing you do for your child that they could learn to do themselves, with money or otherwise. Hand it over, with support. For yourself, ask whether you depend on help that's holding you back.
scenes.caption: HELP, DON'T FUND

scenes.text: Let's put this into a simple timeline. Ages three to five. Coins and counting, the idea that things cost money, and that you sometimes have to wait. Ages six to ten. The three jars, small savings goals, and the difference between needs and wants. Ages eleven to thirteen. An allowance with real responsibilities, comparison shopping, and compound interest.
scenes.caption: AGES 3 TO 13
scenes.chapter: What to teach at every age

scenes.text: Ages fourteen to eighteen. A first job, reading a pay stub, a first bank account and debit card, a custodial Roth IRA if they have earned income, how credit works, and scams. Ages eighteen and up. Budgeting on their own, building credit responsibly, choosing insurance, using an employer retirement plan from their very first job, and taking full responsibility for their own money.
scenes.caption: AGES 14 AND UP

scenes.text: Maybe you're watching this and thinking, nobody taught me any of this. You're not alone. A growing number of states now require a personal finance course in high school, but for most adults today, that came too late. Most people learned by trial and error.
scenes.caption: IF NOBODY TAUGHT YOU

scenes.text: The good news is that every one of these twenty five lessons works for adults too. Start with three jars of your own, as automatic transfers. Learn compound interest with a calculator. Check your credit report. Open a retirement account if you haven't. It's never too late to give yourself the money education you didn't get.
scenes.caption: IT'S NEVER TOO LATE

scenes.text: And if you do have kids, nieces, nephews or grandkids, you can break the cycle. The lessons you learn now can become the kitchen table conversations that change your family's future for generations.
scenes.caption: BREAK THE CYCLE

scenes.text: Question one. Should allowance be tied to chores? Families disagree on this. Some pay for all chores, some give an allowance for learning money skills and expect basic chores as part of being in a family, with extra paid jobs available. Either way, the key is consistency and using the money to teach.
scenes.caption: ALLOWANCE AND CHORES

scenes.text: Question two. How much should I tell my kids about our family's finances? Share values and decisions, adjusted for their age. You don't need to share exact salaries with young children, but older teens can benefit from understanding real numbers, like how much the family spends on groceries or housing.
scenes.query: Parent and teen talking at table
scenes.caption: HOW MUCH TO SHARE

scenes.text: Question three. What if I'm not good with money myself? Then learn together. Watching a parent learn and improve is a powerful lesson. You don't need to be perfect. You need to be honest and willing to grow.
scenes.caption: LEARN TOGETHER

scenes.text: Question four. When should my child get a debit card or a credit card? Many families start with a debit card linked to a teen account around the early teenage years, with parental controls. A credit card usually comes later, often as an authorized user first, and then their own card in early adulthood, used for small purchases paid in full every month. The goal is practice with guardrails before the stakes are high.
scenes.query: Teen with debit card at store
scenes.caption: DEBIT OR CREDIT CARD?

scenes.text: Question five. Should I pay for my kids' college? That's a personal choice, and many families help in some way. But many financial planners suggest prioritizing your own retirement savings first, because students can borrow or earn scholarships for college, but nobody lends you money for retirement. A five twenty nine plan is one tax advantaged way to save for education if you have room in your budget.
scenes.caption: PAYING FOR COLLEGE

scenes.text: Quick recap. Angle one, the numbers. Money is earned, save first, compound interest, interest works both ways, price versus value, opportunity cost, budgeting with an allowance, understanding a paycheck, and owning versus renting.
scenes.caption: THE NUMBERS: 1 TO 9

scenes.text: Angle two, the psychology. Wait for what you want, don't compare, money isn't a secret, small mistakes are cheap tuition, enough is a number, money is a tool, generosity, and wealth is quiet.
scenes.caption: THE PSYCHOLOGY: 10 TO 17

scenes.text: Angle three, the playbook. Open accounts early, credit basics, negotiate, protect what you have, start something, spot scams, the family plan, and not everything is handed over.
scenes.caption: THE PLAYBOOK: 18 TO 25

scenes.text: The best inheritance isn't money. It's knowing how money works. Pick one lesson from each angle and share it with someone you love this week. If you want the full plan, it's in my playbook, linked in the description. And tell me in the comments, what's one money lesson you wish someone had taught you as a kid? I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
